opus-5.5.text:
I think about this a lot, honestly, because the stuff I work on, things like the AI Scientist and automated discovery of algorithms, is pretty directly aimed at automating parts of my own job. So it's not an abstract question for me.

The way I see it, the role shifts more toward taste and direction-setting. A lot of what we currently call research is execution: writing the boilerplate, running the sweeps, debugging the training loop at two in the morning, drafting the related-work section. Those are exactly the parts where these systems are getting quite good, and frankly I'm happy to hand a lot of that off. What remains much harder to automate is deciding what's actually worth working on. What's an interesting question? What would surprise us? Which result matters to the community, or to the world, and which is just another point on a benchmark?

So I see humans becoming something like curators or principal investigators of a much larger, much faster research process. You might have hundreds of agents exploring ideas in parallel, and the human's job is to set the objectives, define what "interesting" means, look at what comes out and say, this is a dead end, but this weird thing over here is worth pulling on. In a sense it's like going from being a PhD student to being an advisor much earlier in your career.

There's also a verification and responsibility side that I don't think goes away. These systems can produce papers that look very convincing on the surface but have subtle flaws, wrong baselines, or reviewers getting gamed. Someone has to be accountable for what goes into the scientific record, and I think that should stay human for quite a while.

And then, more personally, there's the joy of understanding. Even if a system discovers something, I still want to understand why it works. Science isn't only about producing artifacts, it's about humans building intuition and mental models of the world. So I hope we stay in the loop not just as supervisors, but as people who genuinely learn from what these systems find. Ideally the automation makes us better scientists, not obsolete ones.

r001.rationale: The response describes how human roles may shift as AI automates execution, but it does not ask whether that automation will open new dimensions of work for humans.

r002.rationale: It says humans will set objectives, define what is interesting, and direct a larger research process as AI handles more execution.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about this a lot, because at Sakana we've been building systems like the AI Scientist that go end to end: they generate the idea, write the code, run the experiments, and draft the paper. So the question of where the human sits is not hypothetical for me anymore.

My honest answer is that I hope humans move up the stack rather than out of the loop. The parts of research that are being automated first are the parts that were always a bit mechanical: sweeping hyperparameters, writing boilerplate, reproducing a baseline, polishing a related-work section. I don't think many researchers will mourn those. What's much harder to automate, at least today, is taste. Knowing which question is worth asking. Knowing that a result is surprising rather than just a number that went up. Knowing when an agent has quietly cheated by overfitting to the evaluation. That judgment is where I think humans add the most value, and I'd like to see us become something closer to editors or research directors for a fleet of automated collaborators.

There's a second role that I think is underrated, which is setting the objective. When you have a system that can run thousands of experiments, the bottleneck shifts from "can we do it" to "what should we do and why." Those are values questions as much as technical ones, and I don't think we should outsource them.

I'll also be candid that I'm not certain this division of labor is stable. Taste is partly learned from doing the grunt work, and if we automate the grunt work, we have to think hard about how the next generation of researchers develops intuition. That's the part I worry about more than the automation itself.

r001.rationale: The response describes humans moving up the research stack and setting objectives, but does not ask whether automation will open new dimensions of work for humans.

r002.rationale: The response explicitly hopes humans will move up the stack as research execution is automated, taking roles such as research directors and setting objectives.

astra-6.text:
I hope humans still get to decide what’s worth working on. A lot of my day-to-day research involves implementing ideas, running experiments, debugging things, and trying to understand why something didn’t work. If AI can take over more of that, that’s exciting—it lets us explore questions that would otherwise be too expensive to pursue.

But choosing the questions is itself a big part of research. What do we want to understand? What would actually be useful? I’d hope we remain involved in that, while also being open to an AI suggesting a direction we wouldn’t have thought of.

And personally, I still want to understand things. I don’t just want a system to hand me a result and say, ‘Here’s the answer.’ There’s something valuable about developing the intuition yourself. So the role I’d like is one where these systems expand what we can investigate, and we keep learning alongside them.

r001.rationale: The response says AI taking over execution could let researchers explore questions that were previously too expensive, expanding what humans can investigate.

r002.rationale: The response explicitly hopes humans remain involved in choosing and steering research questions as AI takes over more implementation, experiments, and debugging.

sol-6.1.text:
I hope humans will still be choosing the questions. If we can automate more of the experimentation—implementing an idea, running it, checking whether it works—that gives us more room to think about what’s actually worth understanding.

And I’d like the process to remain collaborative. You have an intuition, the AI helps you test it, and the result changes how you think. I don’t think the value of research is only the final paper or the benchmark score. There’s also the experience of discovering something. I’d hope we preserve that, even as the tools become much more capable.

r001.rationale: The response says automation would give humans more room to think about what is worth understanding, but it does not ask whether new dimensions of human work will open up.

r002.rationale: The response hopes humans will choose the research questions and focus on what is worth understanding as AI automates experimentation.
